prd.name: BedTerm MVP
prd.overview: An iOS terminal app designed for coding on iPhone. Users SSH into a Mac mini or Linux box and run Claude Code, Codex CLI, or any terminal tool — with a special keys bar that makes Ctrl combinations, arrows, and Escape comfortable on a touchscreen. The product differentiator is the mobile keyboard experience for terminal input, not the SSH feature count.

requirement.name: SSH Connection
requirement.description: Connect to a remote Linux or macOS host over SSH with standard authentication methods.
requirement.rule: User can enter a hostname and port to connect.
User can enter a username for authentication.
User can authenticate with a password.
User can authenticate with an SSH private key.
A valid connection opens the terminal session and displays the remote shell prompt.
A failed connection shows a descriptive error message without crashing.

requirement.name: Terminal Display
requirement.description: Full terminal emulation rendering ANSI escape sequences, VT100 control codes, colors, and cursor positioning correctly.
requirement.rule: ANSI color codes (16-color and 256-color) render with correct foreground and background colors.
VT100 cursor movement and positioning work correctly.
Clear screen sequences repaint the terminal viewport correctly.
Running vim or nano displays the editor UI correctly, including status lines and cursor positioning.
Running top or htop displays the process list with live updates.
Long lines wrap correctly within the terminal width.

requirement.name: Special Keys Toolbar
requirement.description: A slim toolbar pinned above the system keyboard (and above the direction pad — see R11) that exposes the keys most essential to terminal use that are absent from the iOS keyboard. The toolbar is deliberately minimal — only [ESC], [CTRL], and [TAB] — to keep the input area light and uncrowded.
requirement.rule: The toolbar displays exactly three keys: [ESC], [CTRL], and [TAB]. No other keys (no arrows, no extras) appear on the toolbar.
The toolbar stays visible when the system keyboard is shown and when it is hidden.
Tapping [ESC] sends the escape key (e.g., to exit insert mode in vim).
The toolbar uses the iOS 26+ Liquid Glass material — translucent, depth-aware, responsive to the content scrolling beneath it — instead of an opaque bar.

When the system keyboard is visible, the toolbar rides directly above the top edge of the keyboard — moving up with the keyboard as it presents and back down as it dismisses — so the keys stay reachable without a gap between the keyboard and the toolbar.
When the system keyboard is not visible, the toolbar floats above the bottom safe-area inset, anchored above the direction pad (R11).
The toolbar fits within the available safe area without overlapping the terminal view, the direction pad, or the system keyboard.
Tapping [↑] sends the up arrow key to the terminal (e.g., for shell history). Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [↓] sends the down arrow key to the terminal. Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [←] sends the left arrow key to the terminal. Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [→] sends the right arrow key to the terminal. Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [TAB] sends the tab character for autocompletion.

requirement.name: Ctrl Combination Mode
requirement.description: Tapping [CTRL] enters a combination mode where the next key press is sent as a Ctrl+key combination. This avoids the need for multi-touch chording on a touchscreen.
requirement.rule: Tapping [CTRL] highlights the key and enters Ctrl-pending mode.
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping C sends Ctrl+C (SIGINT).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping D sends Ctrl+D (EOF).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping Z sends Ctrl+Z (SIGTSTP).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping L sends Ctrl+L (clear screen).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping A sends Ctrl+A (beginning of line).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping E sends Ctrl+E (end of line).
If no key is pressed within a short timeout, Ctrl-pending mode cancels and [CTRL] returns to its normal state.
Tapping [CTRL] again while in pending mode cancels the pending state.

Tapping [CTRL] sends the literal Ctrl key code when tapped twice in quick succession, for programs that need a bare Ctrl press. Deferred — a Unix PTY has no byte for a bare Ctrl press; revisit if real usage demands it.

requirement.name: Basic Terminal UX
requirement.description: Standard terminal app conventions for copy, paste, scrolling, text selection, and dark mode.
requirement.rule: User can select text in the terminal and copy it to the system clipboard.
User can paste text from the system clipboard into the terminal.
User can scroll up and down through terminal history with touch gestures.
Scrolling pauses auto-scroll; when scrolled to bottom, auto-scroll resumes and follows new output.
The terminal and app UI use a dark color scheme by default.
Terminal text renders in a monospace font.
Landscape orientation. Dropped from MVP — iPhone target locks to portrait. Revisit if real usage demands it.

requirement.name: Host Key TOFU
requirement.description: Trust-on-first-use host key verification. The first successful connection to a host stores the host's public key fingerprint; subsequent connections compare and warn on mismatch. Added during MVP design as the security baseline for any terminal app.
requirement.rule: On first successful connect, the SHA-256 fingerprint of the remote host key is stored in Keychain, keyed by host:port.
On subsequent connects, the stored fingerprint is compared to the remote host key; a match proceeds silently.
A mismatch shows a full-screen warning with both fingerprints (SHA256:base64) and offers Reject or Trust-new-key (with explicit confirmation).

requirement.name: Local Network Permission
requirement.description: iOS shows a system permission prompt the first time the app sends traffic to a Local Area Network address (RFC1918 IPv4, IPv6 unique-local / link-local, or a `.local` mDNS host). The terminal must handle this prompt gracefully so the first connect to a LAN dev box does not fail before the user can tap Allow. Loopback (`127.0.0.1` / `::1`) and public addresses are unaffected and bypass this flow.
requirement.rule: Before opening an SSH connection to a LAN host (RFC1918 / ULA / link-local / `.local`), the app first triggers the iOS local-network prompt and waits for the user's response.
Connections to loopback or to public (non-LAN) addresses skip the prewarm and proceed directly to SSH.
While the prewarm prompt is on screen, the Connect action shows a "Waiting for local network permission…" state instead of returning an immediate failure.
If the user grants permission during prewarm, the app proceeds to the SSH connect automatically — no second tap on Connect required.

If prewarm completes with permission denied (or a connect to a LAN host fails with a permission-shaped error), the app shows an actionable error: "Local network access is required to reach <host>. Open Settings to enable it."
The denied-error surface includes an "Open Settings" button that deep-links to the app's Settings pane, plus a "Retry" button that re-runs the connect.
Once a connect has succeeded against a LAN host, subsequent connects skip the prewarm wait and proceed directly to SSH unless the user changes permission in Settings.

requirement.name: App Icon
requirement.description: The app ships with a final designed app icon — not the Xcode placeholder — so it has a recognisable identity on the Home Screen, in Spotlight, and in the App Switcher.
requirement.rule: A final app icon design exists and is shipped at all iOS-required sizes (Home Screen, Spotlight, Settings, Notifications, App Store marketing).
The icon ships variants for iOS 18+ Dark and Tinted Home Screen appearances in addition to the default Light variant.

requirement.name: System Appearance
requirement.description: The app always follows the iOS system appearance — Light when the system is Light, Dark when the system is Dark — for both the SwiftUI chrome and the terminal palette. There is no in-app theme override.
requirement.rule: On launch, the app and terminal render in Light or Dark to match the current iOS system appearance, without any in-app theme picker.
Changing the system appearance while the app is open updates both the app chrome and the terminal palette without restart.
When the system is in Light mode, the terminal uses a light background with dark foreground text and legible ANSI colour mappings.
When the system is in Dark mode, the terminal uses a dark background with light foreground text and legible ANSI colour mappings.
In both appearances, the special-keys bar, Connect form, error text, and disconnect banner meet contrast standards against their background.

Every UI surface, text, icon, border, and accent colour is system-adaptive — no colour in the app remains the same in Light and Dark. Switching system appearance changes the rendered colour of every coloured element.

requirement.name: First Launch Onboarding
requirement.description: On first launch, before the Connection form, the app guides the user through a short onboarding that captures (a) what kind of host they will connect to and (b) whether that host is on the same Wi-Fi or remote. The answers tailor the next screen — a setup tutorial for macOS, or an immediate local-network permission request for same-Wi-Fi targets. After completion, onboarding does not appear again unless the user resets it.
requirement.rule: On the very first launch (no prior completion), the app shows the onboarding flow instead of the Connection form.
Once the user has completed onboarding, subsequent launches go directly to the Connection form.
Step 1 asks the user to pick the host kind: "macOS" or "Other (Linux / dev box / VM)".
Step 2 asks where the host lives: "Same Wi-Fi as my phone" or "Remote (over the internet)".

When the user picks macOS, the next screen is a tutorial covering how to enable Remote Login on the Mac and how to find the Mac's IP address. Tutorial content is to be authored — placeholder copy is acceptable for the MVP shell.
When the user picks "Same Wi-Fi", the onboarding immediately triggers the iOS Local Network permission prompt (rather than waiting until the first connect attempt).
When the user picks "Remote", the onboarding does not trigger the Local Network prompt — that permission is unnecessary for public hosts.
After the final onboarding step, the user lands on the Connection form, with the host kind / location choice persisted for future reference.
The user can go back to the previous onboarding step at any point before finishing, without losing the earlier choice.

requirement.name: Direction Pad
requirement.description: A dedicated, oversized 4-way direction pad — styled like a game controller's D-pad — sits above the special-keys toolbar (R3) whenever the terminal is in focus. Its job is to make arrow input fast and forgiving on a touchscreen: large targets, clear hit areas, and continuous-press repeat for moving the cursor or scrolling through shell history.
requirement.rule: The direction pad is rendered directly above the R3 toolbar — between the terminal output and the toolbar — so it remains reachable without scrolling either area.
Each of the four direction buttons is visibly larger than the keys on the R3 toolbar — sized for confident thumb taps, comparable to a physical game controller's D-pad.
The four directions are arranged in a plus / cross layout (Up on top, Down on bottom, Left on the left, Right on the right) with a clear inactive centre, so the user can navigate by muscle memory.
Tapping Up sends the up arrow key to the terminal (e.g., for shell history).
Tapping Down sends the down arrow key to the terminal.
Tapping Left sends the left arrow key to the terminal.
Tapping Right sends the right arrow key to the terminal.
Holding a direction continuously repeats the arrow input at a steady rate (with a brief initial delay), so the user can hold to scroll history or move the cursor across a long line.
Each direction button shows a clear pressed state (visual depression / highlight) and emits a light haptic on tap.
The direction pad uses the iOS 26+ Liquid Glass material, visually consistent with the R3 toolbar.
The direction pad fits within the available safe area without overlapping the terminal view, the toolbar, or the system keyboard.

requirement.name: Lookin Debug Inspector
requirement.description: Debug builds of the app expose their live view hierarchy to the Lookin Mac client (lookin.work), so the iOS team can inspect SwiftUI / UIKit layout, layer geometry, and view attributes at runtime without rebuilding. Release builds must not include Lookin at all — neither the framework nor any of its symbols ship to the App Store. This is a developer-tooling requirement, not a user-facing feature.
requirement.rule: Debug builds bundle the Lookin server framework, so a running debug instance is inspectable from the Lookin Mac client.
Release builds (TestFlight / App Store) do not link the Lookin server framework and do not expose any view-inspection endpoint.
With a Debug build running on a device or simulator on the same Wi-Fi network as the Mac, the Lookin Mac app discovers the running app and can attach to it.

After attaching, the Lookin client can browse the full SwiftUI/UIKit view hierarchy — the Connection screen, the Terminal screen, the toolbar, the direction pad, and the embedded terminal view — and read each view's frame, bounds, and key properties.

Lookin's presence does not change any user-visible behaviour, layout, performance, or permission prompts in either Debug or Release builds beyond the standard local-network prompt already covered by R7.

bug.current: The app forces Dark appearance at the root, so it renders dark even when the iOS system is in Light mode. The terminal also stays on a dark palette regardless of system setting.
bug.expected: The app and terminal mirror the iOS system appearance — Light in Light, Dark in Dark — with no in-app override. Toggling system appearance while the app is open swaps both the SwiftUI chrome and the terminal palette live.
bug.steps: 1. Set the iOS system appearance to Light (Settings → Display & Brightness → Light). 2. Launch the app. 3. Observe: the app and terminal render in Dark instead of Light. 4. With the app open, switch the system appearance to Dark and back to Light. 5. Observe: the app does not react to the system change.

bug.current: The project has no AppIcon asset — the app launches with the default white/blank iOS placeholder icon on the Home Screen, in Spotlight, and in the App Switcher. No icon design has been produced yet.
bug.expected: A final app icon design is produced and added as an AppIcon asset catalog entry covering every iOS-required size, including Dark and Tinted variants for iOS 18+.
bug.steps: 1. Build and install the app on a device or simulator. 2. Go to the Home Screen. 3. Observe: the app appears with the generic placeholder icon instead of a designed icon.

bug.current: On the first launch, tapping Connect against a LAN host (e.g. `192.168.x.x` or a `.local` host) triggers the iOS local-network permission prompt — but the SSH connect attempt has already started in parallel and fails (timeout / no route) before the user can tap Allow. The user sees a confusing error and must tap Connect a second time after granting permission.
bug.expected: The app should detect that the target is a LAN address, run a permission prewarm to surface the iOS prompt, wait for the user's response, and only then start the SSH handshake. If the user grants permission, the connect proceeds automatically; if denied, an actionable error with "Open Settings" and "Retry" is shown.
bug.steps: 1. Fresh-install the app (or reset its local-network permission in Settings). 2. Open the Connection screen and enter a LAN host (e.g. `192.168.1.10`), port `22`, username, password. 3. Tap Connect. 4. Observe: iOS shows the local-network prompt, and a connection error appears behind it before the user can tap Allow. 5. Tap Allow on the prompt. 6. Observe: the connect does not retry automatically; the user must tap Connect again.
